obtained.how: the reprint posted openly by the Harkness Laboratory of Fisheries Research (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources; the authors' lab) on its own publications page, fetched with getsrc; Fig. 7 read on a 400-dpi page image

bibliography.checked_against: the first page (PDF p. 1: 'Behaviour 137, 61-74', © Koninklijke Brill NV 2000) and Crossref (issue 1)

claims.claim: a smallmouth brood at Lake Opeongo holds ~380 larvae/m² at first feeding (project arithmetic)
claims.source_value: measured mean density within broods at first feeding (9.5 mm TL) ≈ 475–540 fish/m² (Fig. 7b: ~480 small, ~540 medium broods, large overlapping small); the project's ~380 is an assumed 1,000-fish brood over the medium broods' mean area (1,000 / 2.6 m² = 385)
claims.location: p. 69 (PDF p. 9), Results 'Brood dispersion'; Fig. 7, p. 70 (PDF p. 10)
claims.conditions: Jones Bay, Lake Opeongo, Ontario (58.6 km², oligotrophic), 1991–1993; area = minimum convex polygon of 10–15 stones laid around the brood by snorkellers, 10:00–16:00; density = brood size estimate / area; brood categories < 500, 501–1,500, > 1,500; mean areas 0.8, 2.6, 5.8 m² at first feeding
claims.note: the inputs are right but the arithmetic answers a different question: the ratio of a guessed brood size to a mean area is not the mean density, which the paper reports directly in Fig. 7b. Use '~500/m² at first feeding' (read off Fig. 7b). Density did not differ among brood-size categories at any phase (F2,81 = 2.31, p = 0.29).

claims.source_value: measured mean density at the early juvenile phase (18.5 mm TL, just after metamorphosis) ≈ 30–45 fish/m² (Fig. 7b), and ~80–115/m² in late larvae (14 mm); the project's ~27 is 1,000 fish / 36.7 m²
claims.location: p. 69 (PDF p. 9), Results 'Brood dispersion'; Fig. 7, p. 70 (PDF p. 10)
claims.quote: Upon reaching metamorphosis, dispersion averaged 14.8, 36.7 and 64.1
claims.conditions: the 14.8, 36.7, 64.1 m² areas are the early-juvenile (18.5 mm) points of Fig. 7a for small, medium and large broods
claims.note: use '~30–45/m² just after metamorphosis' from Fig. 7b; the authors stress that density 'declined sharply before metamorphosis' (Summary)

claims.claim: young smallmouth disperse from the nest at about 28 mm (Opeongo)
claims.conditions: mean total length of the fourth developmental phase observed (after swim-up 9.5, pre-metamorphosis 14.0, post-metamorphosis 18.5 mm); lengths at age differed slightly among years with temperature

claims.claim: after two to three weeks with the male the fry disperse (Scott et al. 1997 and Friesen & Ridgway 2000, via Ridgway et al. 2002)
claims.source_value: Friesen & Ridgway give no two-to-three-week figure: males 'provide sole parental care that can range from 19 to 45 days' (citing Ridgway 1988; Ridgway & Friesen 1992), and broods 'remain in limited areas in the nearshore environment for many weeks'
claims.location: p. 62 (PDF p. 2), Introduction; p. 70 (PDF p. 10), Discussion
claims.quote: provide sole parental care that can range from 19 to 45 days
claims.conditions: the 19–45 days is the whole care period; the paper does not split it into egg/embryo and free-swimming phases
claims.note: the 'two to three weeks' must come from Ridgway et al. 2002 or Scott et al. 1997 (check those entries); citing Friesen & Ridgway 2000 for it is wrong, or say '19–45 days of care (Friesen & Ridgway 2000, citing Ridgway 1988)'

notes: Other useful values: 72, 92 and 76 nests in South Jones Bay in 1991–93, of which 47 %, 77 % and 86 % reached first feeding; mean brood size at first feeding 495, 1,910 and 1,570, distributions skewed to small broods (Fig. 3); first exogenous feeding from 2, 16 and 18 June; broods disperse from the nest at dawn and regroup at dusk (Fig. 2); nest density 0–6 per 100 m of shore. Brood size had no effect on foraging, agonistic behaviour, nearest-neighbour distance or density — the authors infer food is not limiting under parental care.
